claim: Self-interruption is a major, under-studied component of task switching. Across 889 hours of observed task switching from 36 individuals in three high-technology information-work organisations, self-interruption is a function of organisational environment and individual differences AND of external interruptions already experienced; open-plan environments raise it. People are significantly more likely to self-interrupt in order to RETURN to a central working sphere (mean 23%) than to a peripheral or other one (17% and 19%), and to return to solitary work (23%) over a communication event (16%).
source: Dabbish, Mark & Gonzalez, CHI 2011, 'Why Do I Keep Interrupting Myself?: Environment, Habit and Self-Interruption' — primary PDF read at ics.uci.edu/~gmark/
label: verified
bearsOn: attention, task switching, and what a drift event actually means
actionable: labelling. NOT ALL SELF-INTERRUPTION IS DRIFT — a meaningful share is people returning to their real work. This is independent support for 'neutral' as a first-class label (ADR-0047) and a warning against reading every tab switch as failure.

claim: Average dwell on a single screen before switching is roughly 47 seconds; returning to a task after an interruption costs roughly 23-25 minutes.
source: attributed to Gloria Mark; primary source ics.uci.edu/~gmark/chi08-mark.pdf NOT YET READ
